title: Harmonic functions and harmonic conjugates
terms: Laplace equation; harmonic function; harmonic conjugate.

exposition.text:
A twice continuously differentiable real function is harmonic if u + u = 0. The real and
xx yy
imaginary parts of an analytic function are harmonic. A harmonic conjugate v of u makes u + iv
analytic and must satisfy v = u , v = −u .
y x x y
On a simply connected plane domain every harmonic function has a global harmonic conjugate,
unique up to an additive real constant; on domains with holes this can fail. To construct one,
integrate a Cauchy–Riemann equation, retaining an unknown function of the other variable,
then determine it from the second equation.
Harmonic functions are closed under real linear combinations, but generally not under products
2 2 2
or nonlinear compositions. For instance, ∆(u ) = 2|∇u| when u is harmonic, so u is harmonic
on a connected domain only when u is constant.

question.text:
3 2
Let f = u + iv be entire with u(x, y) = x − 3xy + 2x and v(0, 0) = 5. What is v(1, 2)?
(A) 1 (B) 3 (C) 5 (D) 7 (E) 9

solution.text:
3 2 3
The given real part is Re(z + 2z). Hence v = 3x y − y + 2y + C. The initial value gives
C = 5, and at (1, 2) this is 6 − 8 + 4 + 5 = 7.

question.text:
Which harmonic function on C \ {0} has no single-valued harmonic conjugate on that entire
domain?
√
2 2 x
2 2
(A) x (B) y (C) x − y (D) log x + y (E) e cos y

solution.text:
The logarithmic radius is the real part of a local logarithm, whose conjugate is the angle.
The angle increases by 2π around the origin and cannot be globally single-valued. The
other functions are real parts of globally entire functions.

question.text:
2
Let u be a real harmonic function on a connected open plane domain. If u is also harmonic,
which conclusion follows?
(A) u must be identically zero.
(B) u must be constant, but need not be zero.
(C) u can be any affine function.
(D) u can be any harmonic polynomial.
(E) u must have no zeros.

solution.text:
2 2 2 2 2
Differentiation gives ∆(u ) = 2(u + u ) + 2u∆u = 2(u + u ). If both functions are har-
x y x y
monic, this vanishes, forcing both first derivatives to be zero. Connectedness then makes u
constant. Every real constant meets the assumptions, including zero.

Since 1/z = (x − iy)/(x + y ) is analytic on the punctured plane, its imaginary part
